1:
The chapter opens by naming a Persian as the LORD's anointed, and the commentators feel the strangeness of it before they explain it. Ellicott observes that the word is none other than Messiah, and that here alone is it laid on a heathen king; it had not yet narrowed to the sense it carries in Daniel, having been used of Saul, of the house of David, and even of Abraham. What is claimed, on his reading, is that this deliverer would rule by the grace of God as truly as David did, and not merely be called a servant as Nebuchadnezzar was. Gill grants the title without material oil: appointment and fitness make the anointing, not the horn. Wesley compresses the same thought into three verbs — designed, separated, fitted.

Calvin will not let the difficulty pass so quickly. The name belonged to the kings of Judah because their kingdom was an image of Christ's, and it is therefore startling to find it resting on a worshipper of idols. He concedes what history allows: this king revered the God of Israel and reckoned him highest, yet was never moved by sincere affection of the heart, and never forsook his superstitions. So the title is granted for an office and a season, not in perpetuity; he discharged for a time the work of a redeemer, avenging the church and freeing it. From this Calvin draws his point. God so values the salvation of his people that for one such benefit a stranger is called his Messiah.

Henry supplies the history the prophecy outruns. He assembles what the pagan writers report — the disputed birth, the infant exposed and saved by a herdsman's wife, the war with Croesus that ended in the taking of Sardis and made a poor prince rich to a proverb — and dates the oracle two centuries before Babylon fell. He also refuses to read the promotion as a compliment. Xenophon made this conqueror the pattern of a virtuous ruler; other historians call him haughty, cruel, bloodthirsty. The preference was for Jacob's sake, and Henry adds a maxim about it: the wealth and power of this world God has seldom seen fit to entrust to his own, so many are the snares that attend them, and has rather put such things into other hands to be employed for them.

Over the loosing of the loins the readings divide. Clarke simply renders it ungird. Ellicott allows either a general figure of weakening or a specific one of disarming, since the sword hangs from the girdle. Henry takes it both ways — divesting kings of dignity, or of vigour — and finds the letter of it in Belshazzar, whose joints were loosed at the writing on the wall. Calvin weighs the two and chooses the belt of royalty over the sinews, because a promise to gird follows a few verses on and the contrast should be allowed to stand. On the doors, Ellicott distinguishes the two leaved ones of palaces from the gates of cities; Clarke turns to Herodotus for the hundred of brass, and for the river gates left open on the night of the feast, without which the invaders would have been shut in the channel and taken as in a net.

The crooked places are a textual crux. Clarke finds the received word hard to account for and follows the Greek to mountains, noting two manuscripts that support the change, and quotes Ovid on bidding the swollen hills sink down. Ellicott prefers to smooth the dwelling places, meaning simply that obstacles go. Gill levels the hilly ground as pioneers do. Calvin, seeing nothing new in the verse, notes only that money is the sinews of war and that a captain out of the poor Persian mountains needed the buried treasure the next verse promises.
3:
What the promised hoard was, and why it lay in darkness, is answered three ways. Gill repeats a rabbinic tale: Nebuchadnezzar, grudging his wealth to his heir, sank it in brass vessels in the bed of the Euphrates and turned the river over them, and on the day the temple was ordered rebuilt the Lord showed the place. He then leaves legend for Pliny and counts the plunder of Asia — gold by the ton, silver by the hundred thousand talents, the great cup of Semiramis. Clarke prints the same Latin, converts the metal into sterling at over a hundred and twenty million, and pauses on that cup: at fifteen talents it weighs twelve hundred pounds, no drinking vessel but the bowl cups were filled from. He adds a plainer reason for the darkness, that householders buried coin beneath their floors for fear of thieves. Ellicott wants no legend: the wealth of the city and the fall of Sardis account for the spoil, whose purpose was that the conqueror read his victories as a token of protection. Wesley says only that such things had long lain secret.

On whose account it was done the commentators agree and then diverge in emphasis. Ellicott presses on the words servant and chosen: they show the ideal people is meant, the true assembly rather than the nation in its outward standing, and that world history is ordered with a view to it. Gill turns the clause forward, making the named deliverer a figure of one called later for the elect. Calvin hears God address the prince coldly — you shall have your victory, but my regard is for my own, and for their sake nations are put under you. He then asks why they are called servants at all, and answers that no one earns the honour; free choice makes them what they are, and obedience is its end.

Calvin will not stop at the local case. Since the church is kept safe by hidden methods while empires change hands, he retells what Josephus reports of Alexander before Jerusalem: tribute refused, a march begun in fury, the high priest going out in his robes, and the conqueror leaping down to prostrate himself, explaining to a puzzled officer that he worshipped not the man but the God whose figure had met him in a dream at home. The city came away freer than before. Calvin notes what the prediction forestalled: left alone, a man so given to superstition would have credited his idols and despised the captives as slaves.

The girding is read as a deliberate reversal of the opening ungirding. Ellicott says so in a line, taking it for strength given where kings were stripped of it; Calvin makes the same pairing and draws his conclusion, that soldiers have no courage but what is lent them, that weapons decide nothing unaided, and that no victory falls out by chance. Wesley says the man was made strong and active and disposed for war. Henry, hearing the bare declaration that there is none else, finds it aimed at two dangers: the idolatry the prince inherited, and the habit of universal monarchs of accepting worship themselves, which he thinks accounts for no small part of how idols began.

The knowledge is to run from sunrise to sunset, the axis Gill notes takes in the inhabited world as the other does not. Wesley lists three proofs — the foretelling long before, the success given, the overruling of a pagan heart. Calvin admits the promise was not kept at once: few then saw whose hand it was, but the report passed from neighbour to neighbour and was fixed in lasting records, so that what ingratitude buries still shines, unseen only by the blind. Delitzsch sets the commission under its final purpose, the redeeming of one people and the turning of the nations.
7:
Clarke reads the declaration about light and darkness as aimed at a named religion. The Magian system of Persia, in which the prince was probably raised, held two supreme, co-eternal and independent causes always at war, the author of good called Light and of evil called Darkness. Against it, Clarke says, the prophet makes both creatures and instruments, leaving no power of either kind outside the one God. He grants that some Persians held the evil principle subordinate and destined to be overcome. To date the doctrine early enough he goes to Xenophon, where an officer who has threatened a captive he loves excuses himself by claiming two souls, a philosophy learned from that wicked sophist, Love.

What the created evil is, no one leaves loose. Clarke keeps it narrow: war and its miseries, so that as darkness is the privation of light, war is the privation of peace. Ellicott says the words have no bearing on the insoluble problem of the origin of evil; what stands opposed to peace is suffering, not sin. Calvin fights on two fronts. Against those who make God the author of guilt he answers from the shape of the sentence, since peace is set opposite affliction and not opposite righteousness. Against schoolmen who allow that famine comes from God but deny it when the stroke falls by human hands, he answers that wicked men are raised up as instruments, their malice used, not inspired. Gill spreads the pair across every register, from the first day and the eclipse to blindness, hardening and the last punishment; Wesley says in a line that every comfort and calamity comes from that hand alone.

Whether the heavens are asked or commanded divides readers of the next verse. Calvin knows the view that a form of prayer is inserted for the waiting faithful, and rejects it: God is still the speaker, ordering heaven and earth into service, the imperative being the ordinary prophetic one standing for a future. He notes how bleak the alternative looked to the captives, wrath above and chastisement below, so the two quarters holding nothing but threats are commanded to yield salvation. Gill also refuses to hear a petition, noting that Aben Ezra and Kimchi heard an address to the angels. Ellicott sees a new heaven and earth, righteousness both rain from one and crop of the other. Clarke hears a psalm of the restoration imitating this passage, insists that mercy and truth meeting cannot be mere consequences of a return from exile, and reports the Targum reading the opening earth as the rising of the dead.

Who is warned off is disputed. Clarke has the prophet forestalling countrymen who resented rescue promised rather than captivity spared, and adds Kimchi's view that the words strike the Babylonian king who drank from the temple vessels. Calvin calls that forced, and rejects a gentler reading contrasting God's willingness to be questioned with a father's refusal. His own is plainer: impatience under delay. Wesley turns it outward to any who would hinder the appointed man, telling murmurers to quarrel with their equals.

On the figure itself the readings converge. Delitzsch notes how naturally it came, one word serving for the shaping God and the potter, and hears the woe as rebuking faint-heartedness. Ellicott would drop the supplied verbs and let the clause stand in apposition, a potsherd among potsherds, and finds two kinds of presumption in the two questions, one querying the work, the other declaring the workman handless. Calvin refuses an emendation turning the shards into craftsmen, and observes that Paul takes the image up a level, arguing eternal election where the prophet argues this life. To say the hands are wanting, he adds, charges the maker with sloth or ignorance. Gill and Ellicott close from the other woe: no one interrogates his parents about the terms of his own birth.
11:
Everything here turns on whether the words about asking and commanding invite, or land the last stroke of the rebuke. Clarke settles it by the text. Following the Greek he drops a letter from the participle and ties it to what precedes, and on Secker's authority takes the Chaldee verb, with its interrogative prefix, so the whole reads as two indignant questions: do you interrogate me about my children, and direct me in the work of my hands? Ellicott concedes that the received text says the opposite, calling men to consult the Holy One rather than heathen oracles about the future; but he judges a slight alteration more coherent, since questioning and commanding are what the murmurers were doing.

Henry takes the received text and builds on it. Two things open to captives who had made peace with delay: consult the word, asking the prophets and the watchmen how long; then seek by prayer. The verb that sounds imperious he defuses with a distinction — command me, not by prescription but by petition — adding that requests may be earnest and expectations confident so far as grounded on the promise. We may not strive with our Maker by complaint, but may wrestle with him by fervent prayer. Henry knows the other construction and reports it fairly, that some read the clause as a question carrying the reproof forward; but he keeps the promise, noting that complainers assume authority over God. Gill agrees, hearing leave to enquire and to press for performance.

Calvin is on the other side, and lists what he will not have. He rejects the reading that makes God waive his right and allow more questioning than men allow each other, and sets aside a second, that the exiles are wretched because they never ask what is intended for them. His own keeps the sentence whole as the application of the two figures just used: a son may not dispute with his father, clay may not argue with the potter, and less tolerable still is prescribing how the Father shall treat his sons. He hears God defending his workshop, refusing to be dragged from the throne to a human bar. Wesley asks in one line whether men will not allow God the liberty they take themselves.

The appeal to creation backs the argument. Ellicott compresses it: the Creator is also the Ruler, supreme in history as in nature. Gill notes the Targum's addition that the earth was made by the Word, taking the clause as proof the promise can be performed. Calvin will not leave it as bare power. He turns it into an argument from less to greater — if the wisdom shining in heaven and earth governs the world, it surely takes peculiar care of a household, and will not let its own family be scattered; and he brings in the sparrow that does not fall unpermitted. Delitzsch reads the stretch as calming exiles whose fears the conqueror's career had increased rather than lifted.

Over the raising up in righteousness the readers divide again. Wesley glosses it most justly, to punish the Babylonians and plead the oppressed cause; Henry keeps that but adds the performance of promises. Calvin rejects both the punitive sense and the sense that the man would reign justly, insisting the word means fidelity, since God displays his rectitude chiefly in saving his people. Delitzsch agrees, tracing the upheavals to an interposition love alone determined. Ellicott makes it the answer to the murmurers, proved by the city rebuilt and the exiles home, owing nothing to a conqueror's usual greed. On who is meant, Clarke is blunt that this evidently concerns the Persian; Gill grants that and says it is chiefly of Christ. Calvin ends where the ransom clause does: conquerors take a price or impose terms, this one did neither, which shows whose will was at work.
14:
Gill fixes the address first: the feminine pronouns show the words go neither to the Persian nor to Christ but to the church, and he cites Kimchi for Jerusalem. Ellicott marks a new section and measures its advance. The same three peoples had earlier been handed over as a ransom for Israel's release; here they arrive of their own accord, proselytes in self-imposed bondage, addressing to Israel the supplication that belongs elsewhere to God. He is precise about what each brings: two send the produce of their labour, the Sabaeans, strong but not rich, the labour itself. Clarke, less interested in which peoples, suspects a metonymy for wealthy nations at large, and dwells on their height, citing an historian preserved by Bochart and the Greek rendering, tall men. He adds that a long tally of manuscripts supplies a conjunction the received text lacks.

Calvin finds a first instalment paid. The tributary countries lay under Persian rule, and out of their tribute the temple was rebuilt, a literal beginning; the rest waited for a king who could subdue flinty and untameable hearts. He then guards the promise from misuse. Rule is ascribed to the church only because the preaching committed to her is the sceptre by which her Head displays his power, and none submits to her beyond where the obedience of faith joins the ministry of doctrine. Wesley reads a double fulfilment, wealth returning to a rebuilt city and, more fully, nations entering the church that began there, the captives coming willingly. Delitzsch sets the scene under one heading, judgment clearing ground for the fulness of the Gentiles.

Then comes the exclamation about a God who hides himself, and whose voice it is is disputed. Delitzsch is definite that it is not the heathen still speaking but the church answering their confession, the prophet lending his mouth as she breaks into amazement at a God who steers the nations by ways no eye can trace. Ellicott lays both options out without choosing, the wondering homage continued or the prophet alone surveying unsearchable ways. Wesley assigns it to the prophet; Gill hesitates between the prophet reporting his own experience and the church reporting hers.

What the hiding is divides them further, and Calvin clears ground by rejecting two readings. The Jewish commentators, he says, make it a hiding from the nations and a revealing to Israel; that is exactly where Clarke lands in his one line, and where Gill's first sense goes. Christian interpreters, he adds, offer something ingenious but far-fetched, that the hidden God is Christ, divinity concealed under weak flesh. His own is austerely practical: God hides when he refuses help and does not answer, and the epithet Saviour beside it proves the subject is aid, not essence. Gill keeps the other sense in reserve, a God invisible in nature and unsearchable in judgment, and Wesley agrees that the counsels are past finding out. Ellicott answers historically — through the long exile he had seemed negligent or unable, and only afterwards was the Strong one seen to have worked throughout.

The turn to the shaming of idol-makers strikes Clarke as abrupt in two ways, in sentiment and construction, the lines running out from the short measure into two long distichs; he notes too that one clause has lost its subject, which the Greek supplies. Delitzsch reads the perfects as an ideal past and pauses on the noun rendered salvation, which means not rescue but removal into a wide place, into freedom and gladness; he disputes Knobel's dating of the plural for eternities. Calvin turns the contrast against a temptation: seeing the wicked at ease, the afflicted suspect favour, neglect, or blind chance; but present appearances are no measure of power. Gill narrows the promise to a remnant until the last conversion; Ellicott leaves the closing phrase as it stands, ages upon ages.
18:
Ellicott reads the clause about establishing the earth as preparation for habitation: not a waste but the scene of human action, and admires the grandeur of the thought. Calvin knows a narrower reading, that the earth means Judea, and puts it aside for an argument from less to greater. If the ground was fixed so men might be fed by its produce, it was made the more surely to house a church; and as long as the earth lasts the church lasts with it. He also meets the objection. The creation account uses this very word of the earth at the beginning, when it was waste and empty; but the prophet describes the purpose, not the first moment.

Calvin pushes the decree wider than his own party. Because the earth was appointed for men to dwell in, God feeds even the wicked and bears crimes that would else have ended the race; states and settled orders survive among barbarians on the same footing, and where he turns a country barren with salt the rule holds that the ground be inhabited. He adds that the repeated declaration is no claim about bare essence but a mark distinguishing this God from idols, since superstitious men grant one God and then imagine him as they please. Gill assigns the speech to the Son, marking him off from gods who made nothing. Clarke adds a textual point, that an old manuscript and the versions prefix a particle, giving a reason rather than a statement.

The denial of speaking in secret sets Clarke off on his fullest note. Heathen answers came from deep obscure caverns; he cites the Sibyl's cave hewn in the Euboean rock, Strabo on the hollow at Delphi with its narrow mouth, and Diodorus on the chasm beneath the shrine. Oracles clustered in mountainous country full of clefts, he observes, because their horror and gloom served the lying priests. Gill and Wesley say the same briefly, contrasting muttering out of the belly with a law given audibly before a whole people, nothing afterwards spoken in a corner.

The verse's second half gives Clarke a sharper contrast. Cicero's verdict on the Delphic responses: partly false, partly true by accident, partly so twisted the interpreter needs an interpreter. The famous instance is the answer to the king marching against the very conqueror this chapter names: cross the river and you will destroy a great empire. He took it for a promise, fought, and destroyed his own — whichever way it fell, the oracle stood. Not one prediction of the prophets, Clarke says, is framed that way. Calvin allows only that an allusion to the groves and tripods appears likely. Ellicott sets the contrast elsewhere, against the hidden God of the earlier exclamation: the self-revealing had gone on all along in the daylight of history and the law written on men's hearts, seekers sent to a world of order and not to chaos.

Calvin turns the clause into a defence of the written word against those calling it a nose of wax to keep others from reading it. He answers with the lamp for the feet and the surer prophetic word, conceding what lies behind the charge: Scripture is in places dark. That belongs to our dullness, not the text; the blind may not accuse the sun because they cannot look at it. Wesley takes the other clause, that none was told to seek for nothing, as promising recompense for work appointed. On who is summoned, readings part. Henry keeps them literal, the refugees Cyrus released, Jews and others, called to hear why wood overlaid with gold can neither hear nor help — that the old womb of idolatry might become its grave. Gill denies that outright and makes them the Gentile remnant of grace; Delitzsch keeps both ends, a fulness of the nations drawn out of the whole mass.
21:
The last challenge to the idols draws two notes, textual and theological. Clarke finds three readings of the verb: the received let them consult, the Greek let them know, and an old manuscript's let them come together by appointment, which he prefers. Gill wants gods, makers and worshippers summoned to produce a prediction between them. Calvin lets them bring what they have, confident nothing survives comparison with the law and the prophets, and adds that the redemption in view takes in the empire's fall as well as the captives' release, as Wesley also does. Ellicott stops at the double title, whose two attributes, justice and salvation, are commonly thought incompatible in human dealing; the invitation rests on their being joined.

That invitation is the widest thing in the chapter. Delitzsch parses the two imperatives, the first exhorting and the second promising, finding a will bent on the conversion of all and their salvation through it, resting only when it has its object. Calvin marks the turn: until now only the Jews were addressed; the wall is down. He makes it an indictment, since nothing is baser than refusing one's own rescue, and ignorance does not excuse it — men who prefer flattery are not merely mistaken but insincere. Clarke notices that the Targum makes the object of the looking the Word. Gill takes the imperative pastorally, listing what must be looked off first: idols, creatures, one's own doings and tears, even one's graces.

Then the oath, the highest conceivable asseveration on Ellicott's reckoning; being God, Gill notes, he could swear by no greater. Calvin asks why an oath was needed and answers that the calling was new and hard to believe; the condescension strikes him, that to cure distrust God offers his own name as pledge, and unbelief an oath cannot satisfy is the more disgraceful. He draws a rule from it: no saint or creature may be named in a sworn appeal. Clarke reports that the Targum distinguishes the saying that goes out from the personal Word that swears. Wesley catches the force of the word that will not return, comparing an ambassador come home to his prince with nothing done.

On the universal homage they differ over how much has happened. Delitzsch insists the bending will not be forced. Ellicott says the faith of one people becomes the religion of mankind, though on the prophet's own terms that people keeps its nationality. Calvin insists the outward act is meant, not the inward alone, against those claiming an upright heart while bowing to idols, since no soul is given to God while the body is consecrated elsewhere. He then concedes how far off fulfilment lies. The knee is bent wherever the preaching is obeyed, but many still resist, so the prophecy waits; Paul rightly carried it to the judgment, what belongs to that kingdom not being confined to one stage of its course.

Who speaks the confession about righteousness and strength is disputed. Clarke, after listing variants over a pronoun and a number, proposes the words are the Persian's own, citing his decree acknowledging the kingdoms were given him. Ellicott hears the prophet catching a confession made in a far-off time; Gill and Wesley put it in every convert's mouth, righteousness not inherent but received. Calvin notes that commentators differ and keeps to believers, warning that bare knowledge that God exists is not faith. At the close he meets an expected objection — if the nations are called, has the ancient choice failed? — answering that the remnant of adoption was always the true Israel and the grafted nations became Abraham's children, so the covenant stands and none may boast of birth. Ellicott finds the germ of the later thought of union, the Lord as the region in which men live; the seed, for Gill and Wesley alike, is Israelites indeed of either stock.
